weakness: The only transport primitive was a two-finger pinch on the plate's thin, slanted rim lip followed by lifting that edge. With a realistic 0.4 kg plate the pinch slips immediately (36 'dropped' events in 10 seeds, success 0/10). The pipeline had no non-prehensile fallback: closed fingers pushing from inside ride over the shallow rim cone, pushing from outside requires putting the hand on the cabinet side where there is no room, and tilted-finger pushes swept the arm into a neighbouring bowl.
how_found: Questioned F1 (the plate is light enough to lift by its lip). In simulation it weighs 11 g, 30x lighter than a real plate, and the whole strategy rested on that number.
why_missed: I picked the strategy by probing the simulated object and kept whatever moved it; the probes all used the simulated mass, so 'lift by the lip' looked reliable and I never asked whether it scales to a realistic weight. Pushing had been tried first and abandoned for geometric reasons, so no push primitive survived to fall back on.
fix: None accepted. Tried six repairs: drag-in-hops (pinch, lift the edge 2-8 cm so the far edge stays on the table, drag 8-16 cm, release, re-detect), different pinch-angle orderings and speeds; best 0.5 on v1 with base dropping to 0.7. Hops are bimodal (either ~10 cm of progress or a slip with none) and the episode step budget runs out. Pipeline reverted to the round-0 version.
general_rule: Before committing to a grasp-and-lift strategy for an object, check that it still works when the object's mass and friction are scaled to real-world values, and keep a non-prehensile or support-sharing fallback whose required force does not depend on grip friction.

weakness: The pipeline treated the goal region as a fixed place to put the plate and only chose the least-occupied point inside it. When a movable cup stood in the middle of the region, every candidate point overlapped it, so the plate was dropped onto or against the cup and ended tilted or pushed out (0/10).
how_found: Questioned A3/D2 (some part of the goal is free). A small low block (rejected6) was simply shoved aside by the plate (0.6), so I used a taller, heavier movable object that cannot be shoved or covered.
why_missed: In the nominal scene the goal region was empty except for a nearby cheese box, so choosing the clearest point inside it always worked; I designed the target choice to avoid obstacles, not to remove them.
fix: Added clear_goal(): if the best target point still has negative clearance, find the movable object (a name in objects(), not a fixture part) blocking it, grasp it, and place it on a free table spot that is clear of other objects, of the whole goal region (not just the chosen point) and of the plate's carry corridor, and within comfortable reach. A first version kept the spot clear of only the chosen point and the cup landed where the plate later had to go (0.7 -> 0.9 after fixing).
general_rule: Before placing an object at a goal, check that the goal area is actually free; if it is occupied by something movable, relocate the blocker to a spot clear of the whole goal area and of the planned path first.

weakness: The goal-clearing step from round 2 assumed any blocker can be picked up with a top grasp. A 10 cm wide box (wider than the 8 cm gripper opening) could not be grasped, so the goal stayed blocked and the plate was dropped onto the box (0/10). Two hidden weaknesses showed up during repair: the 'plate is lifted' check (detected height above rest) was fooled when the plate came to rest on top of another object, and a pushed-away blocker that ended near the plate's swing path knocked the hanging plate out of the pinch.
how_found: Read the new clear_goal() code and questioned the assumption it introduced (the blocker fits between the fingers). Wide flat things such as boxes, books or cutting boards are common on real tables.
why_missed: The fix in round 2 was written for the one blocker I had just seen (a cup), so the removal primitive was chosen to suit that object and not checked against the gripper's size limit.
fix: clear_goal() now compares the blocker's smaller horizontal side with the gripper span; if it is too wide (or the grasp fails) it is pushed away with the closed fingers (wide finger face against it). The push direction is the one with the shortest travel that ends clear of other objects, of the whole goal region and of the plate's carry corridor, with a reachable start and end; if none qualifies the limits are relaxed. The carry loop now checks that the plate followed the hand (displacement ratio), not only that it is above the table, and the push is scored to end far from the corridor because the dangling plate swings up to a diameter away from the hand.
general_rule: When a skill has to handle an arbitrary object (remove, grasp, move), check the object's size against the gripper's capacity and keep a non-grasping alternative, and confirm that a carried object is really attached by checking that it moved with the hand.

weakness: The rim pinch only considered whether the planner could reach a rim segment; it never looked at what stood around the plate. With four cans 3 cm from the rim, most pinch approaches were refused, the remaining ones (on the cabinet side) carried the plate across the cans, and the dangling plate came to rest on top of them (s_break 0.4, from 0.6 with three cans).
how_found: Questioned E1/A2 (the space around the rim is free for the open fingers and for the swinging plate). Real tables are cluttered, and a pinch on a wide object needs room outside its edge.
why_missed: In the nominal scene the only neighbours were a bowl on one side and the cabinet on another, and trying 8 pinch angles was enough to find a free one. I treated failed approaches as something to retry at other angles, not as a sign that the surroundings had to be changed.
fix: Added declutter(): before the first transfer (and again whenever no rim pinch works) every small movable object within 5 cm of the plate rim or inside the plate's carry corridor is picked up and placed on a free spot (clear of other objects, the goal region, the plate and the corridor). The pick-and-place code was factored out of clear_goal(). A first version only decluttered reactively after all pinches failed; that kept the cans in the carry path (0.5). Doing it before the transfer gave 0.8-0.9.
general_rule: Before manipulating an object, clear small movable clutter from both the volume the gripper needs around the grasp point and the volume the object will sweep while carried; do not rely on trying other grasp angles.

weakness: The pinch point was a hard-coded radius (6.7 cm) and depth (5 mm) tuned on the nominal plate. On a plate scaled to 0.7 the pinch point lies outside the plate and every grasp closed on air (0/10). After deriving radius and depth from the measured bounding box, a second limit showed up: the scaled lip is only 1.3 cm tall, and the grip site cannot go much lower than 1.2-1.7 cm above the table before the finger tips hit it (the planner refuses). The pads therefore barely overlap the lip and the plate slips out when lifted.
how_found: Questioned B3 (fixed size). A scale of 1.3 (rejected1) did not break it, because a constant radius still lands on the wider rim; the smaller side was the real weakness.
why_missed: I tuned the constants by probing one plate. The bigger-plate test passed, so I wrongly concluded that the size assumption was harmless and never tested the smaller side.
fix: None accepted (pipeline reverted). The six repairs are listed in v5.yaml; the best reached 0.5. A low, thin lip needs a different primitive (a side or angled pinch, or a push) that the top-down pinch cannot provide.
general_rule: Derive grasp points and depths from the object's measured size rather than constants, and before relying on a grasp check that the part to be gripped is taller than the gripper's minimum clearance above the support surface; test size changes in both directions.

weakness: Every pinch needs a vertical top-down approach with the 20 cm long hand aligned with the rim's radius. A fixed board 7.5 cm above the table over the far half of the plate makes every such pose collide (0/10, 'no rim grasp' 40 times). The pipeline has no grasp that works from the side or at an angle, and no way to pull the plate out from under the board first.
how_found: Questioned E1 (the space above the rim is free). Shelves, cupboard bottoms and other robot links often cover part of an object on a real robot.
why_missed: The nominal scene had nothing above table height near the plate, so I only reasoned about the footprint of the hand (the fingers), not about the hand's full length at the height where it sits.
fix: None (unsolved). A sweep of the planner over all rim angles and hand yaws found no collision-free pinch pose. Recovering would need a new primitive (an angled or side pinch, or a hook-and-pull of the rim) that this pipeline does not have.
general_rule: When choosing a grasp, check that the whole hand (not just the finger tips) fits in the free space above the grasp point, and keep at least one grasp or contact primitive whose approach direction is not vertical.
